claims.statement: src/progress.rs owns a single process-wide `static MULTI_PROGRESS: LazyLock<MultiProgress>`, and `get_progress_bar(length, style)` is the only helper that adds a bar to it, so bars created by the CLI, by GraphQL mutations and by MCP actions all stack in one render. The module also re-exports indicatif's `MultiProgress`, `ProgressBar` and `ProgressStyle` so `use super::progress::*;` is sufficient for consumers; no code calls `MultiProgress::remove`, and only `mcp::run_action` and `info::main` call `finish_and_clear()`.

The CLI entrypoint creates exactly one bar at startup (`get_progress_bar(0, get_none_progress_style())`), prints the version banner through it, and hands that same `&ProgressBar` to every subcommand `main()`, which may restyle it, set its length and tick it. Hosts without a TTY build their own bar instead: `get_progress_bar(0, get_none_progress_style())` for GraphQL settings mutations and MCP actions, `ProgressBar::hidden()` for spawned GraphQL actions, web upload handlers and most unit tests.

Three progress styles share the `⠋⠙⠹⠸⠼⠴⠦⠧⠇⠏` spinner and `━╸━` progress chars: none (spinner + `wide_msg`), count (`pos/len [bar] speed elapsed (ETA)`, used by import-dats) and bytes (`bytes/total_bytes`). `start_action(bar, msg)` sets the message, forces the none style and enables a 100 ms steady tick; `stop_action(bar)` clears the message and disables the tick. Because the tick is state on a shared bar, callers that start one must stop it — archive, chdman, ctrtool, nsz, xso, gdi, iso, wbfs, rvz and `util::compute_system_completion` all pair the two.

`run_blocking(progress_bar, length, work)` is the bridge from a synchronous, CPU-bound format crate to the async bar: it clones the bar, moves the closure to `spawn_blocking`, resets the bar to the bytes style with `length` (the input bytes the crate will consume) and hands the crate an incrementing callback. A panic in the blocking task surfaces as the distinct message "Conversion task failed" (JoinError), separate from the crate's own error mapped via `anyhow::Error::from`. Callers: gdi, nsz, xdelta, xps, xso.

Every user-facing line goes through nine categorized helpers in src/progress.rs — `print_header` (◆ bold cyan), `print_subheader` (▸ bold), `print_info` (ℹ dim), `print_success` (✔ green), `print_warning` (⚠ yellow), `print_error` (✖ red bold), `print_skip` (↪ dim), `print_action` (→ dim), `print_separator` — each a `ProgressBar::println` with fixed icon and indent. The project rule is never to call `progress_bar.println(...)` directly from a subcommand or format module; the only surviving direct calls outside progress.rs are the two donation-footer lines in `info::main`, immediately followed by `finish_and_clear()`.

Startup builds an env_logger from `OXYROMON_LOG_LEVEL`, captures its filter level before wrapping, installs `LogWrapper::new(multi, logger).try_init().unwrap()` as the global logger so `log::*` records are drawn through the MultiProgress, then re-applies the captured level with `log::set_max_level(level)` so the env var rather than the bridge decides verbosity. This is what keeps log lines from tearing animating bars apart and keeps server diagnostics on the terminal.

Under `oxyromon mcp` stdout carries the MCP JSON-RPC channel and nothing else may write to it, which is why every helper in progress.rs and every log macro renders to stderr (the indicatif/env_logger defaults; nothing in src/ sets its own ProgressDrawTarget). `src/mcp.rs` documents the rule at the top of the module and `import_roms` carries a guard comment where a stray `println!` used to live, reporting per-file import errors with `print_error` + `print_info("Continuing")`. The stdio integration test proves the split by spawning the real binary with `stderr(Stdio::null())` and `OXYROMON_LOG_LEVEL=off` and parsing every stdout line as JSON-RPC.

Under MCP the bar is a machine-readable progress source, not a visual one: `run_action` builds a bar, labels it with `start_action`, and when the caller supplied a `progressToken` spawns a poller that samples `position()`, `length()` and `message()` every 400 ms and forwards only changed state as `notifications/progress`. Subcommands keep ownership of the bar (style, length, message) while the bridge only reads it; afterwards `stop_action` + `finish_and_clear` clean up.

src/prompt.rs wraps four dialoguer primitives (`FuzzySelect` with the fuzzy feature, `MultiSelect`, `Confirm`, `Editor`) in thin functions: `select_opt` returns `Result<Option<usize>>` where `None` means dismissed rather than unmatched, `select` converts that `None` into `bail!("Failed to get user input")`, `multiselect` returns selected indices, `confirm(default)` renders "Proceed?", and `editor` opens an editor (only for `import-patches --name`). Every wrapper attaches the context "Failed to get user input", which is what surfaces when there is no TTY.

The domain prompt helpers share one shape — resolve candidates from the database and only ask when there is a real choice: `prompt_for_systems` returns the whole set when `all` is set or the list is empty; `prompt_for_system` / `prompt_for_system_like` auto-pick a single match and `bail!("No available system")` on zero; `prompt_for_systems_like` returns `vec![]` on zero; `prompt_for_games` returns as-is when `all` or `len() <= 1`; `prompt_for_game` / `prompt_for_rom` auto-pick one and `bail!` on zero; `prompt_for_parent_romfile` returns `Ok(None)` on zero and ranks candidates by descending `jaro_winkler(path, game name)`.

`prompt_for_roms` is the outlier: it inserts a literal "None" at index 0 with that index as the default and shifts the chosen index back with `roms.remove(i - 1)`, so it can legitimately return `Ok(None)`. All three of its call sites are in import_roms and each feeds the result into an `unwrap()` (`rom_game_system.unwrap()`, `rom_game.unwrap()`), so answering "None" or dismissing the list panics the process instead of skipping one file — any new caller must handle `None` before unwrapping.

Batch subcommands gate selection on argv: when `--system` is present the targets are resolved by name-glob and deduped (`resolve_systems_by_name_like` in sort-roms, check-roms, convert-roms, purge-systems; inline find-and-dedup in export-roms) with no prompt, and only its absence falls through to `prompt_for_systems`. Other decisions prompt independently of that gate: rebuild-roms asks arcade-only systems plus a merge strategy when `--merging` is absent, convert-roms/export-roms `select` a format when `--format` is absent, download-dats `multiselect`s Redump systems unless `--all`, import-irds/purge-irds resolve `%PlayStation 3%` without `--system`, config resolves named systems, and import-patches walks system → game → ROM.

Destructive CLI work confirms before committing: sort-roms prints a `Summary:` of planned moves then `if answer_yes || confirm(true)?` commits the transaction and performs the renames, else rolls it back; purge-roms applies the same `answer_yes || confirm(true)?` gate around its trash/orphan/foreign deletions. Both read `-y/--yes` into `answer_yes` at the top of `main()`. rebuild-roms declares `-y/--yes` but never reads it, and still calls `select()` for the merge strategy when `--merging` is absent, so a non-interactive rebuild-roms blocks on that prompt.

`import-roms --unattended <none|skip|first>` (default `none`) decides the fate of files needing a human: with `first` ambiguous ROMs are ranked by `jaro_winkler` against the file name and the best taken, with `skip` (or `first` with no name to rank against) the file is reported `Multiple matches, skipping` and returned as `MatchState::Skipped`, with `none` the user is prompted via `prompt_for_roms`. A PS3 jukebox folder with no `--system` warns and skips when unattended, otherwise prompts. `import-irds`/`purge-irds` derive a `headless` boolean from `--system`: headless picks the first parent ROM, purges every IRD game, and requires an exact tag-stripped title match (`unattended_game`) rather than a fuzzy best match, which would silently attach an IRD to the wrong game.

Non-CLI hosts reuse the CLI's own bypass switches rather than new code paths: GraphQL mutations and MCP write tools both synthesize argv containing `-y`/`--yes` for sort-roms and purge-roms, import paths always pass `--unattended` (MCP maps a missing parameter to `first`; the web upload/URL import also defaults to `first`), and import-irds/purge-irds are reached with `--system` supplying headless. MCP layers its own authorization on top: destructive tools are refused via `need_confirm` unless the call carries `confirm: true`, so `--yes` answers the CLI prompt but does not authorize the tool.

Tests must never block on interactive selection: `check_roms` and `common::select_games` call `prompt_for_games(games, cfg!(test))`, so under `cargo test` all named games are resolved instead of hanging on a multiselect. The complementary short-circuit — a single match returns unchanged with `all = false` — is covered directly by src/prompt/test_prompt_for_games_single_match.rs.
